title: Sun Insurance Office v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a fire insurance policy is a contract of indemnity where the insured can recover only to the extent of the pecuniary loss sustained. Over-insurance does not entitle the insured to recover more than the actual loss, and the insurance company may reduce recovery to actual value.
doctrine: A fire insurance contract is a contract of indemnity. The insured cannot recover more than the actual cash value of the property at the time of loss. The purpose of insurance is to indemnify the insured, not to enrich them. Over-insurance does not entitle the insured to profit from a loss.
fullText:
REGALADO, J.:

The issue is the proper measure of recovery under a fire insurance policy when the insured property is totally destroyed.

The Insurance Code provides that the measure of indemnity in property insurance is the extent to which the insured has been damaged. An insurer is not liable beyond the amount of the actual loss sustained by the insured. Fire insurance is a contract of indemnity — its purpose is to compensate the insured for loss actually sustained.

The insured cannot recover more than the actual cash value of the property at the time of loss, regardless of the face value of the policy. To allow otherwise would create a moral hazard and encourage arson.
